analysis.one_liner: Lets banks merge with securities firms by repealing the Glass-Steagall separation of banking and securities.
analysis.headline: The House Banking Committee approved the bill 38-6 and it reached the House calendar in June 1995, but it never received a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tear down the Depression-era wall that keeps banks separate from securities firms. Banks could own securities underwriters through holding companies, and securities firms could tie themselves to banks, subject to Federal Reserve approval and capital tests. The bill also moves bank brokerage departments under securities regulators, overrides state laws that bar these affiliations, and requires clear warnings that investment products sold at banks are not insured deposits.
analysis.who_benefits: Large banking companies and securities firms that wanted to combine deposit-taking with underwriting, trading, and investment advice. Bank holding companies gain a regulated path to owning securities affiliates; securities firms gain potential access to bank capital and bank customers; bank trust and brokerage departments gain new permitted roles.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 20 of the Glass-Steagall Act, which since 1933 barred member banks from affiliating with securities firms, and allows financial services holding companies to own securities affiliates.

Lets well-capitalized, well-managed holding companies make certain acquisitions and engage in new financial activities without prior Federal Reserve approval, and repeals the requirement that the Fed weigh adverse effects like conflicts of interest and undue concentration of resources when approving new activities.
Brings bank brokerage departments under securities-law 'functional regulation' as registered brokers and dealers supervised by the SEC.

Bars states from prohibiting bank-securities affiliations solely because the securities affiliate engages in specified activities, and lets well-capitalized national banks underwrite municipal securities.
Permits corporate credit cards, allowing credit card banks to issue them where currently prohibited.

analysis.who_pays: If the bill had passed, the federal deposit insurance fund — and ultimately insured depositors and taxpayers behind it — would bear any added risk from banks tied to securities underwriting; the bill itself directs the FDIC to study and charge for that risk. Bank customers would encounter more investment products sold at bank counters, protected mainly by disclosure warnings rather than structural separation. State governments would lose their authority to block such affiliations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Deposit insurance fund, bank customers, states

drawbacks.text: Affiliating insured banks with securities underwriters puts securities risk next to the deposit insurance fund; the bill acknowledges this by requiring the FDIC to study the risks posed to deposit insurance funds and to factor any increased risk into bank assessments.

Repeals the mandate that the Federal Reserve consider whether a new financial activity would cause undue concentration of resources, unfair competition, conflicts of interest, or unsound banking practices before approving it.
Allows officers, directors, and senior executives of a securities affiliate to serve simultaneously at an affiliated bank, and overrides state laws restricting bank-securities affiliations.

The bill's own safeguards — disclosure that securities sold at banks are not FDIC-insured, customer opt-outs on information sharing, and firewall limits on lending to affiliates — rely on disclosure and regulation rather than keeping the two businesses apart.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give banks and securities firms substantial new freedom to combine businesses, which its sponsors framed as competition and innovation. But the concrete gains flow to large financial companies, while the principal risks — strain on the deposit insurance fund and customers confusing investment products with insured deposits — fall on the public. The bill includes real safeguards, including capital tests, firewalls, and mandatory disclosures, but an honest reading is that it trades away structural separation for a disclosure-and-supervision regime managed by the affected firms' regulators.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared both the Banking and Commerce committees and was placed on the House calendar in June 1995, but the House never voted on it, and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. James Leach, chair of the House Banking Committee, introduced the bill on February 27, 1995; it attracted zero cosponsors.
After eight days of hearings, the Banking Committee first ordered the bill reported 29-8 on May 9, reconsidered, and ordered it reported again 38-6 on May 11; it was formally reported on May 18.
The Commerce Committee extended its consideration twice and reported the bill on June 22, 1995, without recommendation.
The bill was placed on the Union Calendar (Calendar No. 74) on June 22, 1995, but no rule was granted and no floor vote ever occurred through the end of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing separation of banking and securities stayed in force through 1996, preserving securities firms' protection from bank-affiliated competitors and keeping securities-underwriting risk away from the deposit insurance fund. The bill's committee-level momentum was preserved on paper for possible revival, but nothing changed in law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Securities firms and the deposit insurance fund

for.role: Financial industry participants seeking to combine banking and securities businesses
for.what_they_did: Pressed Congress through the mid-1990s to repeal the Glass-Steagall separation of banking and securities, the central provision of this bill.

sides.party_line_note: The only votes recorded were in committee: the Banking Committee reported the bill 38-6 after reconsideration, and the Commerce Committee reported it by voice vote without recommendation; the full House never voted, so no party split on the merits is on the record.

industries.note: The bill lets banks affiliate with securities underwriters through holding companies and exempts well-capitalized banks from prior approval for acquisitions. The gain comes with risk shifted toward the deposit insurance fund, which the bill directs the FDIC to study and price.

Securities firms gain the right to affiliate with banks and tap bank-group capital, but they also face new competition from bank-owned underwriters. Their exemption from the dealer definition and their access to affiliation were long-standing industry asks.
The bill preempts state laws that prohibit or limit bank-securities affiliations, removing a layer of state-level control over bank activities.

industries.industry: Bank trust, custody, and brokerage departments
industries.note: Banks may act as custodians and trustees for investment companies and are brought under SEC registration as broker-dealers, expanding their permitted fee businesses, subject to new disclosure and conflict rules.
